newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan watchdog probe includes Nomura itself-source.
newsitem.headline: Japan watchdog probe includes Nomura itself-source.

text.p: Japan's securities watchdog is investigating whether Nomura Securities itself as well as certain executives either compensated clients for losses or funnelled profits to them, a government source said on Tuesday.

Both actions would be against Japanese securities law and individuals found to have violated the law would face a fine of up to one million yen ($8,100) and a maximum one-year jail sentence. If a company is found in violation, the fine is up to 100 million yen ($813,000).

The source said that, depending on the results of raids on Tuesday at Nomura offices, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) could recommend that the finance minister take punitive action against Nomura Securities itself.
"We will make a thorough investigation and will deal strictly with the case," said the source, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Earlier on Tuesday, officials from the SESC and the Tokyo Prosecutors Office raided Nomura's headquarters and several other unspecified locations as part of investigations into suspect deals which came to light earlier this month.

Nomura, Japan's biggest brokerage, admitted on March 6 that two of its directors, who later resigned, had conducted discretionary transactions and funnelled funds to a corporate client in apparent violation of the law.

The government source said that the SESC had decided to search the firm's headquarters while investigations were still underway because of concerns that evidence could be hidden. He said the search could continue on Wednesday.
Nomura said on Tuesday it regretted the raids but would cooperate with investigators.

The source said that the SESC started the special investigation into Nomura's deals last summer after it noticed that the company conducted an unusual transaction in shares in Fuji Bank Ltd, but declined to give further details.

"Whether you see them (Nomura's dealings with the client) as compensation for losses or a funnelling of profits differs according to the point of view, but both would be in violation of the securities law," the source said.

Earlier on Tuesday, deputy chief prosecutor Kunihiro Matsuo told reporters that the raids were in connection with suspicions that former Nomura director Shimpei Matsuki paid 38 million yen ($308,000) to a company run by a relative of a racketeer to avoid disruption of a Nomura annual meeting.
But he declined to comment on any future plans regarding Matsuki and the other former Nomura director, Nobutaka Fujikura.

Earlier this month Nomura's former president Hideo Sakamaki, who resigned from his post to take responsibility for the incident, said he did not believe wrongdoing was systemic in the company, but added he did not know for sure whether any other executives might be involved. ($1=123 yen)
